Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette: Mr. Tran is a 50-year-old South Eastern Asian man who sought help after experiencing persistent symptoms following a traumatic stalking incident that occurred six months ago. A musician by profession, Mr. Tran had been stalked over several weeks, culminating in an intense confrontation where he was physically and verbally attacked. The event left him feeling vulnerable and shattered his sense of safety. Since the trauma, Mr. Tran has developed a pervasive belief that he is weak and that institutions failed to protect him, leading to a profound emotional numbness. He feels as though he should have been able to defend himself better, reinforcing his belief in his own weakness. This internal dialogue exacerbates his fear of going to unfamiliar places where he cannot assess the danger. Mr. Tran's trust in others has eroded, making it difficult for him to feel safe at night or when he is around people who could potentially pose a threat. Mr. Tran's memories of the stalking are fragmented and often relive with full sensory intensity. He describes moments during which fragments of the memory come back suddenly without warning. The vividness and unpredictability of these memories have made it difficult for him to function normally, especially when he is in unfamiliar settings where such memories can be particularly intense. These sudden recollections further deepen his fear and avoidance behavior. The traumatic event has also left Mr. Tran with significant gaps in his memory, making it hard for him to piece together a complete narrative of what happened. This fragmented recall causes him distress, as the missing pieces feel like unhealed wounds that continue to reopen unexpectedly. The intensity of these memories exacerbates his sense of vulnerability and reinforces his belief that he is weak and unable to protect himself. Mr. Tran's occupation as a musician has been profoundly affected by his condition. He often avoids performing in new venues or playing for unfamiliar audiences, fearing that he cannot predict potential threats. This avoidance has led him to miss several important performances and gigs, impacting both his income and his sense of self-worth. What frightens Mr. Tran most is the fear of being alone and unprotected, a sentiment that only grows when he reflects on the traumatic event and the institutional failures that occurred. Mr. Tran's emotional numbness manifests in his interactions with others, making it difficult for him to form new relationships or rebuild trust with former colleagues. His sense of isolation has intensified over time as he avoids social situations where memories might resurface. The constant vigilance at night and watching others closely for signs of potential harm have taken a toll on his mental health. The cycle that Mr. Tran finds himself in is particularly distressing. His negative appraisals-feeling weak and emotionally numb-lead to heightened threat perceptions, which then trigger more intense and unpredictable memories. These memories further reinforce his sense of vulnerability and weakness, creating a self-perpetuating loop. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was the realization that he could no longer avoid the constant fear and emotional numbness, especially as it began to impact his professional life. He is most hoping for a way to regain control over his memories and fears, to rebuild his sense of safety and trust in others, and to once again feel connected to the world around him.
